\[
E(x) = \frac{1}{\lvert P(x) \rvert} \sum_{p \in P(x)} y_{t(p)}(x)
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(E(x)\): The edge probability at pixel x
- \(y_t(p)\): The edge patch that tree t predicts at position p
- \(P(x)\): The predictions whose edge patches cover x

The image is turned into channels. They hold color in CIE LUV, the gradient magnitude, and the gradient in 4 orientations, at two scales. Differences between cells of a 5 x 5 grid in a patch add self-similarity features. Each tree of a random forest looks at a patch of 32 x 32 pixels. It predicts a whole edge patch y of 16 x 16 pixels, a structured output, instead of one label. The model has 8 trees. At each position, every 2 pixels, 4 of them run, so the edge patches overlap and every pixel collects many votes. E(x) averages the votes of the set P(x) of predictions that cover pixel x, which gives the edge probability. Dollar and Zitnick trained the forest on the BSDS500 images, where people drew the edges of objects. So it learned which changes in an image people call edges, and it ignores texture that Canny would mark.
